title: Twelve stones (Joshua 3–4)
hookLine: the Jordan parts, and they pile stones so their children will ask what they mean

cards: "What mean ye by these stones?" That question is the reason for today's story, and nobody has asked it yet. The people stand at the Jordan, and the river is not low: it "overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest."
Joshua tells the priests to carry the ark of the covenant to the edge. Not to wait. To walk in.

Their feet touch the water, and upstream the river rises up in a heap. The priests stand on dry ground in the riverbed while all the people pass over. Then Joshua gives an odd order: go back in, and pick up some rocks.

teach.h: A STONE FROM WHERE THE PRIESTS STOOD.
teach.b: One man from each of the twelve tribes takes a stone on his shoulder, from where the priests stood.

Before anyone lifts one, Joshua tells them why, in the King James Bible: "That this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones?"
The answer is a story: the waters were cut off before the ark. They carry them to Gilgal, where Joshua sets them up. The text mentions no writing on them.
They're a heap of river rocks in a strange place, and that's the point.

teach.h: BUILT TO MAKE A CHILD ASK.
teach.b: They're built to make a child stop and ask. A memorial that works only when someone asks, and someone else tells the story.
The chapter says it again near the end: "Then ye shall let your children know, saying, Israel came over this Jordan on dry land." In between is a stranger detail.
Verse nine says Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the river, where the priests had stood, "and they are there unto this day." One pile on the bank, where anyone can see it.

teach.h: A SECOND PILE UNDER THE WATER.
teach.b: Another in the riverbed, under the water once it flows again. The text never explains the second pile. Some readers hear a reminder that part of what carries a person stays out of sight.

teach.h: ALL THE PEOPLE OF THE EARTH.
teach.b: And the chapter's last verse widens the circle: it was done so "that all the people of the earth might know the hand of the LORD."

how: Some Christians keep a stone, a cross or another small object as a reminder of a time they believe God carried them through, and some families make a habit of telling those stories to their children.

games.q: you're one of the priests carrying the ark. the Jordan is over its banks. Joshua says go. what happens?
o: you wait on the bank until the water parts.

games.why: the river stops only when "the feet of the priests that bare the ark were dipped in the brim of the water." the step comes before the dry ground.

practice: Look for something that marks a time you were carried through: a ring, a card, a hospital bracelet, a chipped mug, or one that comes to mind.

Hold it, or picture it, and ask what story it would tell if a child picked it up and said, what's this? If you pray, give thanks for the river you crossed; if you don't, simply hold the memory and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Twelve stones. River rocks set up at Gilgal, so that children would ask what they mean and hear the story.
